description: Composite five-row by six-column figure comparing grain-boundary segmentation methods on polycrystalline microscopy images. Column headers read Raw image, Expert label, MatSAM, OTSU, Canny, Watershed; the MatSAM column is enclosed in a red box in every row, marking it as the proposed method. The five rows are five datasets, each identified by a badge in the lower-left corner of its raw micrograph: PI-1, SS, HEA, PI-2 and LCS. Raw panes are grayscale optical micrographs of equiaxed grain structures, except PI-2 which is olive/greenish-yellow with uneven illumination; SS and PI-2 show strong large-scale brightness gradients, HEA shows scattered dark dots, and LCS has the coarsest grains. Expert label panes give the reference boundary network. MatSAM outputs visually reproduce the expert boundaries in all five rows. OTSU fails where lighting varies: in SS it traces the illumination gradient, in PI-2/SS it yields a roughly elliptical region and dense speckle, and in LCS it adds isolated false blobs inside grains. Canny over-segments into cluttered broken boundary fragments, and Watershed leaves large blank, unsegmented areas in the SS, HEA and PI-2 rows. No scale bars, magnifications or numeric values are printed anywhere in the figure.

subfigures.description: Raw pane: pale low-contrast optical micrograph with faint grain boundaries, badge 'PI-1'. To its right: Expert label boundary network, the red-boxed MatSAM result, then OTSU, Canny and Watershed boundary maps. MatSAM closely matches the expert network; OTSU and Canny retain most boundaries but Canny is noisier and Watershed is coarser.

Raw pane: grayscale micrograph with strong uneven illumination, badge 'SS'. OTSU output is a large approximately circular region following the brightness gradient rather than the grains; Canny produces a dense over-segmented network; Watershed leaves large blank areas; the red-boxed MatSAM pane reproduces the expert grain boundaries.

Raw pane: light gray micrograph with scattered small dark dots (likely pores or second-phase particles), badge 'HEA'. MatSAM and expert label show comparable dense small-grain boundary networks; Canny is fragmented and noisy; Watershed leaves part of the field unsegmented; OTSU shows a fine but incomplete network.

Raw pane: olive/greenish-yellow micrograph with marked uneven lighting, badge 'PI-2'. OTSU output is dominated by black speckle/clusters that do not follow the grain boundaries, and Watershed captures only a fraction of the structure, while the red-boxed MatSAM pane still recovers a near-complete boundary network.

Raw pane: light gray micrograph with the largest grains and few boundary intersections, badge 'LCS'. MatSAM reproduces the coarse boundary network closely; OTSU shows the boundaries plus small isolated false detections inside grains; Canny keeps the network with slight thickening; Watershed is close to the expert label with minor missing stretches.

observations.observation: The figure is a 5-row x 6-column grid whose column headers are, left to right: 'Raw image', 'Expert label', 'MatSAM', 'OTSU', 'Canny', 'Watershed'.
The five rows correspond to five labelled datasets, each named by a badge in the lower-left corner of its raw micrograph: PI-1, SS, HEA, PI-2, LCS.
The MatSAM column is outlined with a red rectangle in every row, visually flagging it as the proposed method.
The raw-image column contains grayscale optical micrographs of equiaxed polycrystalline grains for PI-1, SS, HEA and LCS, while the PI-2 raw image has an olive/greenish-yellow tint.
In the SS and PI-2 rows the raw micrographs show pronounced uneven illumination (large-scale brightness gradients) across the field of view.
In the SS row the OTSU pane is dominated by one large approximately circular region that follows the illumination gradient instead of tracing individual grain boundaries.
In the PI-2 row the OTSU pane consists largely of black speckle and clusters unrelated to the grain boundary network, and the Watershed pane segments only part of the field.
In the SS, HEA and PI-2 rows the Watershed panes contain large blank, unsegmented regions, whereas the red-boxed MatSAM panes cover the full field with a continuous boundary network.
In the LCS row the raw image contains the coarsest grains of the five datasets, and the OTSU pane shows small isolated false detections inside grain interiors in addition to the boundaries.
No scale bars, magnification values, axis labels or numeric annotation are printed in any pane of this figure.
The caption states the figure presents visual results of MatSAM and rule-based methods on polycrystalline microscopy.
The citing text reports that on the PI-2 dataset MatSAM achieves an ARI of 0.75, outperforming SAM (0.69) and Canny (0.42).
The citing text reports that for the public LCS dataset MatSAM reaches an ARI of 0.96 on 16 test images, compared with SAM at 0.86.

The citing text attributes the failure of OTSU and Watershed in the fourth row (PI-2) to uneven lighting, and notes that for SS, HEA and PI-2 the OM grayscale values vary little between adjacent grains but largely across regions.

The citing text states that MatSAM receives structure-aware points (prior knowledge from rule-based methods) and therefore delivers more accurate and refined recognition results across the five datasets.

measured_quantities: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) for segmentation accuracy (dimensionless, reported in text not printed in figure)
number of LCS test images (16, stated in text)
unreadable_items: No scale bars or magnification values are present/legible in any raw-image pane, so grain size cannot be quantified from the figure
No ARI or other numeric segmentation scores are printed on any pane; the values quoted (0.75, 0.69, 0.42, 0.96, 0.86) come only from the citing text
Panels carry no printed (a)/(b)/(c) labels; row and column identity is inferred from the header row and the dataset badges in the raw images
